events.title: The seven houses ride to the vein-house rather than the red hall
events.body: On the queen's death the seven houses' messengers pass over the empty capital and ride straight to Taigh na Fèithe above the mountain, choosing to settle the succession among the galleries and lot-stones rather than under the house of Catrìona's own roof. No leaf gives the reason; a young scribe of the vein-house later says it felt from the first hour less like a choosing than a homecoming.

events.title: Nine days at the long table
events.body: The heads of the seven houses sit first nine days at the table under the vein-house's north window, and ride up again at every season's turning for five years, while the capital's clerks hold grain prices and boundary pleas unanswered for want of anyone with standing to settle them. At the last sitting the name of Dòmhnall Ruadh of Muileann chrom is spoken and not spoken down again.

events.title: Dòmhnall Ruadh told whose yard he stands in
events.body: An old custodian takes the newly named Dòmhnall Ruadh aside in the vein-house yard and tells him it is the same ground on which Raghnall Ruadh, of his own house, once refused every claimant offered him and shut the door on a season of refused hearths. Dòmhnall Ruadh says only that he hopes to prove a different answer to the same question.

events.title: Dòmhnall Ruadh's household summoned from Muileann chrom
events.body: Riders carry word to Muileann chrom for Dòmhnall Ruadh's wife and two grown sons to come up to Cathair dhearg; he spends his first night as king naming aloud which of his neighbours he trusts to keep his own galleries honestly measured in his absence, troubled more by that than by the crown awaiting him.

events.title: Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned at six-and-fifty
events.body: Dòmhnall Ruadh is crowned at Cathair dhearg nine days after the houses name him, six-and-fifty years old, in a hall his house had never in nearly three hundred years entered as anything but petitioner.

events.title: The king's horse known on the mountain road
events.body: Riding the thirty-nine miles between Cathair dhearg and the vein-house so often in the first years of his reign, Dòmhnall Ruadh is known by his horse before his face, and the road's keepers complain that they never shod one animal so often in one man's service.

events.title: The boundary stone of the shifted stream
events.body: Dòmhnall Ruadh rides down from the capital to Muileann chrom himself to settle a boundary dispute between two households of his own old neighbours, and fixes the stone's place by asking each household's oldest member, separately, where they remember playing as children, rather than by any measuring the vein-house owns.

events.title: The king keeps his seat at the red hall
events.body: Pressed by more than one of the seven heads to move the crown's seat to the mountain, since a king who is master of the vein-house belongs among the galleries, Dòmhnall Ruadh keeps it at Cathair dhearg for the whole of his five-and-twenty years.

events.title: The reeve's entry read out to the king
events.body: Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeve reads him the fair copy of the entry joining the crown to the mastery of the vein-house before it is set to the king's own mark; Dòmhnall Ruadh says it reads less like a new law than a plain account of what has already been true since the morning in the yard, and the reeve agrees.

events.title: The custody-book and the crown's rolls copied onto one shelf
events.body: The vein-house's clerks spend the better part of two years copying the custody-book and the crown's rolls, kept apart under separate roofs for near three hundred years, onto the same shelves in the same hands, until no leaf of either record can be told from the other at a glance.

events.title: The metalworker who cuts the seal
events.body: A metalworker of Muileann dhearg who has never before been asked to cut more than a gallery-marker spends near a season on the new seal's die, complaining that the gold will not sit against the blue as he wishes. Dòmhnall Ruadh, seeing it finished, says he can find nothing in it that is properly his to add.

events.title: Dòmhnall Ruadh buried under the mountain
events.body: Dòmhnall Ruadh is carried, by his own long-standing wish, not to the house of Catrìona's tombs at Cathair dhearg but up to the vein-house, where the custodians dig his grave themselves in a worked-out gallery and lay him with a single unlit lamp at his head, a rite kept for no other ruler before or since.

events.title: Raghnall Òg asks to shorten his own coronation
events.body: At the rehearsal of his coronation Raghnall Òg twice asks the clerks whether the ceremony might be shortened by an hour so that he can see a shire plea before dark, more at ease already with a boundary dispute than with a court's ceremony.

events.title: Raghnall Òg crowned at six-and-forty
events.body: Raghnall Òg is crowned at Cathair dhearg after his father's burial under the mountain, six-and-forty years old, keeper already of the crown's shire pleas.

events.title: The young priest's question at Cnoc bheag
events.body: At the council of the Hawk a young priest rises to ask the elders whether Mòd himself would rather starve a grown flock than see his old handful grown to meet it. The council turns on the question, and the Fed Hawk is named from that day.

events.title: The first barges tie up at Seann Chwen's new mole
events.body: The first coal-barges of the mountain roads tie up at Seann Chwen's finished stone mole where before they only beached on shingle at low water; a rider carrying the news south remarks that he rode the whole way under one seal without troubling to wonder which office he rode for.

events.title: Beathag nic Sheumais builds the Fed Hawk's house
events.body: Beathag nic Sheumais, nineteen at the schism, builds the Fed Hawk's following at Seann Skell on the north coast from four families to a proper school over two decades, within sound of a sea that has never given the island a word of what lies beyond it.

events.title: Beathag nic Sheumais rides south to petition in person
events.body: Rather than trust the asking to a letter, Beathag nic Sheumais rides to Cathair dhearg herself in her fiftieth year and lays the north coast's cold winters before the seven heads without once raising her voice; the council refuses her at length, and she carries the refusal home in her own satchel.

events.title: The fourteen named at the gallery's mouth
events.body: The vein-house sets a stone with the fourteen names of Cill ghlas cut in the order they went down, the youngest a boy of thirteen, the oldest a woman forty years at the same gallery. Households of the mountain take up the custom of leaving their own small stones at its foot on the day of the fall.

events.title: A head of the seven names the fourteen before the council
events.body: Laying the matter of the coal-roads before the king's council, one of the seven heads says plainly that fourteen names on a stone at a gallery's mouth are proof enough the mountain's coal is given up at a real cost, and that no house's quarrel has business stopping it on the road. None of the seven speaks against him.

events.title: The posts driven along the coal-roads
events.body: Coal-carters hired for the season and paid from the roads' own tolls drive posts the length of all four coal-roads through a single autumn, a trellis and a hollow stone cut at every shire joint, without ceremony or a word said over the last post.

events.title: A carter's answer, remembered afterward
events.body: A carter who helped set posts on three of the four coal-roads is asked the next spring what the work was like, and says only that a man can now walk any of them from the mountain to the sea and never lose the road for want of knowing whose it is; his answer outlives the council's own leaf of the debate.

events.title: Mairead nic Aonghais's three tallies
events.body: The keeper of a road-house on the northern coal-road keeps three notched sticks beside the reeve's own tally of the crown's riders: one for every rider through, one for those who thank her by name, and one for those carrying business she judges not worth the horse it rode on.

events.title: The last shieling of Doire uaine
events.body: An old woman drives her last three goats and a lame ewe down from her own shieling in the high pastures of Doire uaine, the last of her country to come down, and tells the priest who meets her at the valley's edge that a place can grow tired of being lived in alone by living things.

events.title: A drover crosses the empty pastures
events.body: A drover taking cattle to the lowland market by the old high road finds the whole stretch of the forsaken shielings of Doire uaine silent from end to end, not a dog barking nor a hearth smoking, and pushes his herd on rather than camp the night on ground nobody is left to grant or refuse.

events.title: Four thousand counted on the salt flats
events.body: The reeve of Ros fhionn's salt fair loses his own count somewhere past four thousand among the carts, pack-mules and children on the flats, and writes the figure down rounded rather than pretend to a precision the crowd never held still for.

events.title: A carter's plain answer
events.body: Asked by a clerk of the red hall why he sells his barley at Cathair mhòr and not the capital, a carter of the southern road answers that a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; the clerk enters the answer as given.

events.title: The quarry face opens on Toll-dubh
events.body: A stubborn seam on the quarry face north of the capital swings inward on nothing and opens on a cold, scentless dark; the quarryman Calum Dubh mac Iain names the shaft Toll-dubh before any other man on the ledge can, and the whole crew falls silent.

events.title: Calum Dubh climbs the stair
events.body: Calum Dubh mac Iain goes down the stair of Toll-dubh alone with a lamp and a paid-out rope while his fellows watch the light dwindle and vanish; he climbs out again, sits a long while on the loose stone, and tells the foreman only that the face must be closed.

events.title: The custody-book takes Calum Dubh's silence as given
events.body: The vein-house's custodians wall the mouth of Toll-dubh within a month and enter Calum Dubh mac Iain's own brief account of the walling exactly as he gives it, adding nothing to fill out what he leaves unsaid.

events.title: The copper-workers' maker's marks
events.body: The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr stamp every cooking pot with its own maker's mark, a leaf, a fish or a plain letter, and the pots go out on every road at once, carried by hands their makers will never meet.

events.title: A saying born of a silent man
events.body: The quarry town takes up a way of speaking of any close-mouthed man, that he has gone down and come up like Calum Dubh, and the saying outgrows him within a generation, applied to men who never went near Toll-dubh at all.

events.title: Ailean measures the temple-ruin's altar
events.body: Ailean mac Dhùghaill lays his cord across the altar-stone of Làrach an Teampaill and finds it faces the central mountains, its back to the sea, a plain fact no teller of the ruin's tales had ever thought worth the mentioning; he says only that he will not guess who set the stone so.

events.title: Birth of Mòrag Ruadh
events.body: A daughter, Mòrag, red-haired and called Mòrag Ruadh, is born into Clann Raghnaill; the custody-book gives the house and the year, for no one yet has cause to write more.

events.title: The farmer's barrowload of stone
events.body: A farmer whose plough turns up stone every spring at the edge of his field meets Ailean mac Dhùghaill at Làrach an Dùin with a barrowload of it, half in earnest asking whether the school will pay for what his own ground keeps giving back; Ailean measures every stone and buys none of them.

events.title: The school judges Ailean's tables
events.body: The school at Dùn thais argues a winter over Ailean mac Dhùghaill's finished tables of the three old ruins and judges only that his measurements stand sound and his caution on their makers sounder still, closing the question no scholar after him could reopen.

events.title: Death of Calum Dubh mac Iain, still silent
events.body: Calum Dubh mac Iain dies in his own house in his sixty-fifth year, well liked in the quarry town for a quiet kindness, having told no living soul, wife, son or scribe, what he saw on the stair under the hill.

events.title: The steward's mistaken tally
events.body: The girl Mòrag Ruadh finds her own small wax-board tally of the hall's candles does not agree with the steward Pàdraig mac Ìomhair's great ledger; he finds the fault his own, a tally-mark set down twice, and sets his sums before her eyes from that evening forward.

events.title: The seven houses name Mòrag Ruadh
events.body: The seven houses of custody, meeting at the vein-house on the death of the old king, send word to Cathair dhearg within the month that the crown will go to the girl of Clann Raghnaill who keeps her own small tally beside the steward's; the custody-book gives four lines and no reason beyond her house and her blood.

events.title: The queen's own book bound
events.body: Mòrag Ruadh has a vellum ledger bound within the month of her crowning, clasped in iron rather than silver at her own asking, and enters the cost of her own coronation feast on its first page, signed under her own name.

events.title: Mòrag Ruadh crowned at nineteen
events.body: Mòrag Ruadh is crowned at Cathair dhearg at nineteen, the youngest ruler the red hall has seen since Eilidh Bhàn, and keeps her own small tally beside the steward's from the first day.

events.title: Tòmas clears the moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag
events.body: The priest Tòmas mac Aonghais spends a month clearing moss from the obelisk above Cnoc bheag with wooden scrapers rather than iron, and finds, once the stone stands bare, letters cut deep and old that answer to no shape the schools' own tables keep.

events.title: The queen asks after the unread stone
events.body: Hearing the report of the cleared obelisk read to her hall, Mòrag Ruadh enters the cost of Tòmas mac Aonghais's oil and vellum into her own book without comment, and asks only whether the priests mean to try the letters again; the answer she is given is that they do not know.

events.title: Ruairidh mac Neacail hangs the catch in the wind
events.body: When Caol shean's salt runs out on the second day of its greatest catch, the shed-foreman Ruairidh mac Neacail hangs what cannot be salted on lines strung the length of the lower town's lanes rather than let it spoil on the strand.

events.title: The queen judges the thousandth year a measure and no more
events.body: Asked by the seven houses whether the vein-house's thousandth year deserves a feast or a fast, Mòrag Ruadh judges between them: one burning on the quay the count began from, no more coal in it than an ordinary hearth burns of an evening.

events.title: The queen's journey to Seann Skell
events.body: Mòrag Ruadh rides down to Seann Skell over roads already hard with the season's first frosts to stand at Cidhe an Diosail for the thousandth year's burning, a week's journey she makes to see the measure kept rather than take a scribe's report of it.

events.title: The queen's entry for the burning
events.body: Where another ruler's book might have set down a verse for a thousand years made into one evening's fire, Mòrag Ruadh's own book gives the cost of the coal reckoned to the vein-house's weights, and beneath it five words: one handful, nothing more.

events.title: Caol shean returns to salting
events.body: The dried catch sells poorly against salted fish, fetching less at market than a middling salted season the year before; Caol shean lays in salt from that year for a catch half again the size of any it has yet taken.

events.title: Birth of Beathag Fhionn
events.body: Mòrag Ruadh's daughter is born at Cathair dhearg and named Beathag before the child is a day old; the queen's book holds one line for the day and the name, set apart from the ordinary sums in a hand less steady than usual.

events.title: The mill-race market opened above Muileann fhada
events.body: The hill-lords of Baile ghorm set a single market at Cnoc bhàn above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada to gather the south-east's scattered trade in one place, its rare good the pearls no other market sells in whole parcels.

events.title: Sìne nic Ruairidh sells a season's pearls whole
events.body: The shore-woman Sìne nic Ruairidh brings a whole season's gathering to the mill-race market's first opening rather than sell it a pearl or two at a time along the road, and a trader of Cathair mhòr pays her more for the lot than she has ever been offered piecemeal.

events.title: Oighrig nic Ailein fixes Baile ghorm's blue
events.body: After ten years changing one thing at a time in her own mordant, the dyer Oighrig nic Ailein finds a mixing that holds Baile ghorm's blue fast through washing after washing; cloth of it is worn within the year at the vein-house's midwinter gathering.

events.title: Birth of Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn
events.body: A son, Ailean, is born at Cathair dhearg to Beathag Fhionn, the queen's daughter, then thirty years old, in the one-and-fiftieth year of Mòrag Ruadh's reign.

events.title: Word of the cough reaches the red hall
events.body: A rider who has ridden the eighteen miles from Muileann dhomhain without stopping to eat brings word of a sickness that closes the throat. Beathag Fhionn, thirty-nine and eleven years at her mother's right hand, sets down the tally she is reading.

events.title: Reeves set at the fords against the cough
events.body: Newly crowned, Beathag Fhionn closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets a reeve at each of the road's six fords with orders to turn back every traveller until the road is released. Chosen mostly from the towns nearest their own crossing, the six hold the road shut for three years, and the cough never crosses west of them.

events.title: The ford-reeve turns back his own brother
events.body: At the crossing nearest Muileann dhomhain, the reeve Seumas mac Coinnich turns back his own brother, who has come to the closed road to reach their dying mother on its far side. He tells him the order holds for every traveller or for none. Their mother dies within the week, and the brothers do not speak again for five years.

events.title: Death of Queen Mòrag Ruadh
events.body: Mòrag Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg at two-and-eighty, sixty-three years crowned, the longest reign the red hall has yet entered. Her own ledger, clasped in iron, is closed on its last sum.

events.title: Beathag Fhionn crowned at two-and-forty
events.body: Beathag Fhionn is crowned in the hall her mother held sixty-three years, forty-two years old and grey already at the temples; the first act set down under her own seal is the closing of the coast road.

events.title: The reeve of Muileann dhomhain walks the lower street
events.body: The old reeve of Muileann dhomhain, who lost a wife and a son to the cough, walks the lower street once a season and writes down which roofs have fallen in since his last walking; the town stands at less than two households in three.

events.title: Three brothers from Caol dhearg come down
events.body: Three brothers, sons of a hill farmer of Caol dhearg, walk down to Muileann dhomhain and take empty houses on the lower street, land already cleared and walls already standing being cheaper than any new house on a hillside.

events.title: A carter's mule lost at Drochaid Ros fhionn
events.body: The road bed of Drochaid Ros fhionn gives way under a salt-carter's mule one wet spring; the mule drowns in its traces and the carter is left standing waist-deep in the Abhainn bheag holding a dripping harness.

events.title: Beathag Fhionn's last question
events.body: Queen Beathag Fhionn dies at Cathair dhearg at eighty-nine, dictating a grain ruling the morning she takes to her bed; her last question to the young scribe beside her is whether the road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain still stands open.

events.title: Ailean crowned at nine-and-fifty
events.body: Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg within the season of his mother's death, nine-and-fifty years old and no longer a young man by any measure the hall can offer.

events.title: The names cut again at Dùn ìseal
events.body: Setting new ancestor-posts in the old ground the season after lightning burns the old ones to their footings, the keepers of Dùn ìseal cut the names again as best their own memories and their neighbours' can give them back.
